concept.name: Poison Message Handling

relationships.description: Connects Poison Message Handling to caching in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Poison message handling isolates unprocessable queue or stream messages—caused by malformed payloads, schema drift, or deterministic business-rule bugs—so they do not loop infinitely and starve healthy traffic.
spark.keyTakeaway: Never let a single bad message block a partition or burn 100% of consumer CPU; bound retries with exponential backoff, then quarantine to a Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) with full error context.

concept.whyItMatters: At-least-once delivery guarantees that any message failing acknowledgment gets redelivered. When a message triggers a deterministic exception (such as `JsonParseException` or `NullPointerException`), naive infinite retries turn one 2 KB poison pill into a self-inflicted outage: Kafka consumer lag spikes to millions, SQS workers spin at 100% CPU, and healthy messages behind the poison pill miss SLAs.
whenToUse: Any asynchronous worker consuming from ordered partitions (Kafka, Kinesis) where one blocked offset stalls all subsequent events for that key or partition.
Shared work queues (Amazon SQS, RabbitMQ, Google Pub/Sub) processing external webhooks or multi-version producer payloads.
Financial, order, or notification pipelines where dropping a failed event silently is unacceptable and manual triage/replay is required.
whenNotToUse: Idempotent, high-churn telemetry or metrics streams where losing 0.001% of malformed samples is cheaper than operating a DLQ replay pipeline.
Transient infrastructure failures (such as a 503 downstream timeout) where the message itself is valid and belongs in a retry topic rather than immediate DLQ quarantine.
Synchronous request/response RPCs where the caller is waiting on HTTP 400/422 and can fix the payload immediately.
keyPoints: Distinguish **transient faults** (network timeouts, DB deadlocks -> retry with jittered backoff) from **poison messages** (schema mismatch, invalid enum, missing required field -> fast-fail to DLQ).
Always cap delivery attempts: e.g., SQS `maxReceiveCount = 3` in a Redrive Policy, RabbitMQ `x-death` header count, or Spring Kafka `FixedBackOff(1000L, 3)` before `DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer`.

Preserve diagnostic metadata on the quarantined message—exception class, stack trace summary, consumer version, original topic/partition/offset, and first-failure timestamp—in message headers or attributes.

In partitioned logs like Kafka, blocking retries (`SeekToCurrentErrorHandler`) halt the partition; high-throughput systems instead use non-blocking retry topics (`orders.retry.1m`, `orders.retry.10m`) leading to `orders.dlq`.
A DLQ without an owner, alerting, and a tested replay/discard runbook is just a silent data graveyard.

examples.title: Kafka partition stall from a schema-breaking producer deploy
examples.scenario: A microservice deploys a change emitting `amount: "N/A"` instead of a numeric decimal on `payments.v1`. Consumers throw `NumberFormatException`, fail to commit the offset, and re-poll the same message every 500 ms.
examples.outcome: Adding a `DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer` that classifies `DeserializationException` and `ConversionException` as non-retryable routes the 1,420 bad events straight to `payments.v1.dlq` with `x-exception-message` headers, restoring 12,000 msg/s partition throughput immediately.

examples.title: SQS visibility-timeout thrashing on a deleted tenant
examples.scenario: A background job queue receives 400 webhook events for a tenant whose account was hard-deleted 10 minutes earlier. Workers throw `TenantNotFoundException` and return the messages to the queue until visibility timeout expires.
examples.outcome: Configuring `RedrivePolicy` with `maxReceiveCount = 3` and `deadLetterTargetArn` moves the 400 messages to `webhooks-dlq` after 3 attempts, cutting worker CPU from 94% to 12% and enabling a one-click redrive if the tenant is restored.

tradeOffs.factor: Strict per-key ordering vs. non-blocking throughput
tradeOffs.pro: Moving a poison message to a DLQ or delayed retry topic immediately unblocks the partition for all other keys.
tradeOffs.con: If a subsequent valid event for the *same* entity key arrives while the earlier event sits in the DLQ, out-of-order state updates can occur.

tradeOffs.factor: Immediate DLQ vs. multi-tier retry topics
tradeOffs.pro: Routing non-retryable exceptions straight to the DLQ eliminates wasted compute and queue churn.
tradeOffs.con: Misclassifying a transient bug (e.g., a 30-second downstream schema cache lag) as permanent forces manual DLQ replay instead of automatic recovery.

tradeOffs.pro: Retaining DLQ messages for 14 days with full stack-trace headers lets engineers patch the consumer and replay safely.
tradeOffs.con: Large stack traces in headers can exceed broker limits (e.g., Kafka 1 MB `max.message.bytes` or SQS 256 KB limit) unless truncated.

failureModes.name: DLQ consumer loop (poisoning the DLQ)
failureModes.description: An automated DLQ redrive job replays messages back to the main topic without fixing the consumer bug or payload, causing an endless ping-pong loop.
failureModes.mitigation: Attach a `dlq-replay-count` header, cap automated replays to 1–2 attempts after a verified deployment, and require manual approval for repeated failures.

failureModes.name: Rebalance storm during synchronous backoff
failureModes.description: A Kafka consumer sleeps 6 minutes (`Thread.sleep`) retrying a poison message, exceeding `max.poll.interval.ms` (default 5 minutes), triggering a group rebalance that hands the exact same poison pill to another consumer.
failureModes.mitigation: Keep synchronous retry backoff well below `max.poll.interval.ms`, or use non-blocking retry topics / `pause()` + `poll()` loops.

failureModes.name: Header overflow on dead-lettering
failureModes.description: Appending full multi-kilobyte Java/Python stack traces on every retry pushes the message past SQS's 256 KB or Kafka's 1 MB limit, causing the DLQ publish itself to fail.
failureModes.mitigation: Truncate exception messages to 1–2 KB in headers and log the full stack trace to centralized observability keyed by `trace_id`.

failureModes.name: Silent DLQ accumulation
failureModes.description: A DLQ fills with 50,000 failed billing events over a weekend because no metric or alert watches DLQ depth.
failureModes.mitigation: Alert on `dlq_depth > 0` (or rate > threshold) via CloudWatch `ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible` or Kafka consumer lag monitors.

commonMistakes: Catching all exceptions and acknowledging (`commit` / `delete`) the message anyway, silently losing production data.
Retrying `JsonParseException`, `ValidationError`, or `400 Bad Request` 10 times with exponential backoff when the payload will never magically become valid.
Blocking a Kafka `poll()` thread longer than `max.poll.interval.ms`, causing endless consumer group rebalances.
Sending messages to a DLQ without recording *why* they failed, forcing engineers to guess the error days later.
Using `enable.auto.commit = true` in Kafka, which can commit the offset of a failed message before recovery logic runs.

sections.content:
## The idea

A poison message is any event or job that a consumer repeatedly fails to process—not because the infrastructure is temporarily down, but because the message itself triggers a deterministic failure (malformed JSON, unexpected Avro/Protobuf schema, missing foreign key, or an unhandled edge case in business logic).

Under at-least-once delivery, failing to acknowledge a message causes the broker to redeliver it. Without a bound on delivery attempts and a quarantine destination, a single poison message creates a head-of-line block in partitioned logs (Kafka) or an infinite CPU/cost loop in work queues (SQS, RabbitMQ).

Robust poison message handling splits error recovery into two paths: **short, bounded retries** for transient faults (5xx timeouts, lock contention) and **immediate or post-threshold quarantine** to a Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) enriched with diagnostic headers.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider an order-fulfillment consumer reading from Kafka topic `orders.created` (`12` partitions, `max.poll.interval.ms = 300000` ms) with `enable.auto.commit = false`:

1. **Deserialization guard**: The consumer uses Spring Kafka's `ErrorHandlingDeserializer` wrapping `JsonDeserializer`. When a producer emits truncated JSON at partition `3`, offset `918442`, deserialization fails before business code runs and routes the raw bytes immediately to `orders.created.dlq` with `kafka_dlt-exception-message`.
2. **Transient vs. permanent classification**: Valid JSON enters `OrderService.process()`. A `SocketTimeoutException` against the inventory API triggers non-blocking retry topics (`orders.created-retry-5s` -> `orders.created-retry-30s` -> `orders.created-retry-5m`). A `ConstraintViolationException` (negative quantity) is marked non-retryable.
3. **Quarantine & alert**: After 3 failed attempts (or immediately for non-retryable errors), `DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer` publishes the record to `orders.created.dlq`, commits offset `918443` on the main partition, and increments `orders_dlq_messages_total`.
4. **Triage & replay**: An engineer inspects the DLQ record, fixes the consumer or patches the payload, and runs a controlled replay CLI that resets `dlq-attempt = 0` and republishes to `orders.created`.

edges.description: Consumer pulls message with manual offset commit / visibility timeout.

edges.label: Retry (N <= 3)

edges.description: Transient errors retry with jittered backoff; permanent parse/validation errors skip retries.

edges.label: Route to DLQ
edges.title: Quarantine with context
edges.description: After N=3 failures (or on non-retryable error), publish to DLQ with exception & offset headers.

edges.label: Ack / Commit

edges.description: Consumer commits the main offset so healthy messages behind the poison pill proceed.

edges.label: Controlled replay
edges.title: Patch and redrive
edges.description: After deploying a fix or repairing the payload, operator redrives quarantined messages.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Broker-native mechanisms: Kafka, SQS, and RabbitMQ
sections.content:
## Broker-native mechanisms: Kafka, SQS, and RabbitMQ

Each major broker implements dead-lettering differently, and knowing the exact primitive prevents subtle misconfigurations:

- **Amazon SQS**: Uses a `RedrivePolicy` (`{"deadLetterTargetArn":"...","maxReceiveCount":3}`). SQS tracks `ApproximateReceiveCount` server-side; once exceeded, the next receive moves the message to the DLQ atomically. Note that SQS DLQ retention starts from the *original* enqueue timestamp unless configured otherwise.
- **RabbitMQ**: Uses a Dead-Letter Exchange (`x-dead-letter-exchange`) and optional `x-dead-letter-routing-key`. A message is dead-lettered when rejected via `basic.nack(requeue=false)`, when its TTL expires, or when `x-max-length` overflows. Consumers inspect the `x-death` header array to count prior failures.
- **Apache Kafka**: Kafka has **no** broker-side DLQ primitive. The consumer framework (e.g., Spring Kafka `DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer` or Confluent `errors.tolerance=all`) is responsible for producing the failed record to `<topic>.dlq` and committing the source offset.

## Retry and quarantine patterns compared

| Pattern | Partition Ordering | Rebalance Risk | Infra Complexity | Best Fit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Blocking in-memory backoff | Preserved | High if > `max.poll.interval.ms` | Low | Short 100–2000 ms transient blips |
| Pause partition + poll loop | Preserved | Low (heartbeats continue) | Medium | Strict per-key ordering required |
| **Non-blocking retry topics** | **Relaxed per key** | **None** | **Medium-High** | **High-throughput microservices** |
| Broker DLQ (`maxReceiveCount`) | N/A (queue) | None | Low | SQS / RabbitMQ task workers |

## Failure modes

Even teams with a DLQ routinely hit four operational traps:

1. **Deserializer crash loop**: If the Kafka `JsonDeserializer` throws *before* your `try/catch` inside the listener, the consumer crashes and restarts infinitely without ever invoking your DLQ publisher. Wrap deserializers in an error-handling wrapper.
2. **Ordering corruption on partial replay**: If `OrderCreated` goes to the DLQ while `OrderCancelled` succeeds on the main topic, replaying `OrderCreated` two hours later resurrects a cancelled order unless you check state versions (`version` / `updated_at`).
3. **Unbounded redrive loops**: Running `sqs start-message-move-task` before deploying the consumer fix simply bounces the same 5,000 messages back to the DLQ.
4. **Schema Registry bypass**: Producers writing raw bytes without schema validation push poison-pill detection downstream to every consumer instead of failing fast at publish time.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Preventing poison messages at the producer
sections.content:
## Preventing poison messages at the producer

The cheapest poison message is the one never published. Enforce contracts at ingress using **Protobuf** or **Avro** with a Schema Registry (`BACKWARD` or `FULL` compatibility mode) so incompatible field types fail during CI or producer serialization.

For JSON over HTTP/webhooks, validate payloads against **JSON Schema** (or Pydantic / Zod) at the API gateway before enqueueing, returning `422 Unprocessable Entity` synchronously to the caller instead of injecting malformed data into asynchronous pipelines.

## Practical checklist

- Disable `enable.auto.commit` in Kafka and wrap deserializers with `ErrorHandlingDeserializer` so malformed bytes never crash the poll loop.
- Classify exceptions explicitly: fast-fail `JsonParseException` and validation errors straight to the DLQ; retry `TimeoutException` / `503` up to 3–5 times with jittered backoff.
- Enrich every DLQ message with `x-exception-class`, `x-exception-message` (truncated <= 2 KB), `x-original-topic`, `x-original-offset`, and `x-failed-at`.
- Set `ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible > 0` (SQS) or `dlq_lag > 0` (Kafka) alerts routed to the owning team's Slack/PagerDuty.
- Document and test a replay script that checks idempotency/versioning before redriving DLQ records.

interviewProblems.title: Poison Message Handling
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Poison Message Handling. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Poison message handling isolates unprocessable queue or stream messages—caused by malformed payloads, schema drift, or deterministic business-rule bugs—so they do not loop infinitely and starve healthy traffic.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Consumer Worker applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Dead-Letter Queue.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Dead-Letter Queue experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Attach a `dlq-replay-count` header, cap automated replays to 1–2 attempts after a verified deployment, and require manual approval for repeated failures.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Never let a single bad message block a partition or burn 100% of consumer CPU; bound retries with exponential backoff, then quarantine to a Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) with full error context.
Avoid trap: Catching all exceptions and acknowledging (`commit` / `delete`) the message anyway, silently losing production data.
Avoid trap: Retrying `JsonParseException`, `ValidationError`, or `400 Bad Request` 10 times with exponential backoff when the payload will never magically become valid.
When to reach for it: Any asynchronous worker consuming from ordered partitions (Kafka, Kinesis) where one blocked offset stalls all subsequent events for that key or partition.
When to reach for it: Shared work queues (Amazon SQS, RabbitMQ, Google Pub/Sub) processing external webhooks or multi-version producer payloads.

putItTogether.title: Putting Poison Message Handling Together
putItTogether.summary: Never let a single bad message block a partition or burn 100% of consumer CPU; bound retries with exponential backoff, then quarantine to a Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) with full error context.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Poison Message Handling before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Adding a `DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer` that classifies `DeserializationException` and `ConversionException` as non-retryable routes the 1,420 bad events straight to `payments.v1.dlq` with `x-exception-message` headers, restoring 12,000 msg/s partition throughput immediately.
